posts.title: How to fix a dripping tap in 20 minutes
posts.excerpt: A dripping tap wastes thousands of litres a year. Here’s the ten-dollar fix, step by step.
posts.content:
A tap that drips once a second wastes more than 10,000 litres of water a year — and in most cases the fix is a worn washer or cartridge that costs less than a coffee. Here is how our plumbers do it.

What you need

  • An adjustable spanner and a flat screwdriver
  • A replacement washer or cartridge (take the old one to the shop)
  • A towel to protect the sink and catch small parts

Step by step

  1. Turn off the water under the sink, then open the tap to drain it.
  2. Prise off the decorative cap and undo the handle screw.
  3. Unscrew the valve with the spanner and swap the washer or cartridge.
  4. Reassemble, turn the water back on and test.

If the tap still drips, the valve seat itself may be worn. That needs a reseating tool — or a quick visit from us.

posts.title: Five signs your water heater is about to fail
posts.excerpt: Rusty water, rumbling noises and lukewarm showers are your heater asking for help.
posts.content:
Most water heaters give plenty of warning before they quit. Catch the signs early and a flush or a new part can add years of life; ignore them and you may be mopping the garage floor.

Watch for these

  1. Rusty or cloudy hot water.
  2. Rumbling or popping sounds as it heats.
  3. Showers that turn lukewarm sooner than they used to.
  4. Moisture or small puddles around the base.
  5. A tank more than ten years old.

A yearly flush removes the sediment behind most of these problems. It takes us about an hour and costs far less than a replacement.

posts.title: A cleaner’s checklist for getting your deposit back
posts.excerpt: The eight places landlords always check — and our cleaners never skip.
posts.content:
After hundreds of move-out cleans, our team knows exactly where inspections focus. Start with these and you are most of the way there.

  • Inside the oven and under the hob
  • Fridge seals and the drip tray
  • Limescale on taps and shower glass
  • Grout lines in the bathroom
  • Skirting boards and door frames
  • Light switches and handles
  • Window tracks and sills
  • Behind the washing machine

Take dated photos when you finish. If there is any disagreement later, they are the best evidence you can have.

posts.title: When to call an electrician (and when you can DIY)
posts.excerpt: Changing a bulb is fine. Here is where our electricians draw the line — for your safety.
posts.content:
Plenty of small electrical jobs are safe for a careful homeowner. Plenty are not. Our rule of thumb: if it involves opening a box that is connected to the wall, switch off at the breaker — and if you are not sure, call.

Usually fine to do yourself

  • Changing bulbs and plug-in lamps
  • Resetting a tripped breaker once
  • Replacing a plug on an appliance cord

Always call a professional

  • Breakers that trip again and again
  • Warm outlets, burning smells or buzzing
  • Adding new circuits, outlets or fittings

Electrical faults are a leading cause of house fires. A fifteen-minute check is always cheaper than the alternative.

posts.title: Winter-proof your pipes before the first frost
posts.excerpt: A burst pipe is the most expensive repair we see each winter. Prevention takes an afternoon.
posts.content:
Water expands when it freezes, and a pipe in a cold garage or crawl space can split overnight. These steps take an afternoon and save a lot of heartache.

  1. Insulate exposed pipes with foam sleeves.
  2. Disconnect and drain garden hoses.
  3. Find your main stop valve and make sure it turns.
  4. Keep the heating at 12 °C or more when you are away.
  5. Open cupboard doors under sinks on outside walls during cold snaps.

If a pipe does freeze, warm it gently with a hair dryer — never a flame — and call us if you see any crack or damp.
